intro_html:
HB 755 and its Senate companion SB 383 have had no committee vote, and bills still pending when the 136th General Assembly ends in December 2026 die. Until a law passes, a Columbus resident deals with AEP Ohio. Its homeowner guide says that if a customer-owned generator is connected to its system, “then your equipment is interconnected”, and walks through an application, an interconnection service agreement, an AC disconnect switch that must be “lockable and accessible to our crews at all times”, a post-installation field verification and a new two-way meter. The process is written for hard-wired rooftop systems, not a device on a plug.

Ohio’s 2022 solar-access law does little for apartments. For condominiums, Revised Code §5311.192 lets an owner install a solar device only on “the roof of” a “solar appropriate unit”, one with no other unit directly above or below it, only where that roof is the owner’s responsibility or the declaration provides for solar devices, and only “unless specifically prohibited in the declaration”. The association keeps the power to restrict size, place and manner. A balcony in a mid-rise building is outside the statute, and renters are not covered at all.

balco.nyc’s calculator models a specific Columbus address and lets you enter the rate from your own bill in place of Ohio’s 18.0¢ average.

faq: Does Ohio's condominium solar law cover balconies?

No. Revised Code §5311.192 lets a condominium owner install a solar device on the roof of a “solar appropriate unit”, one with no other unit directly above or below it, and only unless the declaration specifically prohibits it. A panel on a balcony in a multi-story building is outside its scope.
